decks.title: Moving Charges and Magnetic Field — Part 1: Defining B and the fields of currents
goals: Describe Oersted’s observation and define the magnetic field B from the force F = q(v × B)
State the Biot–Savart law in vector form and use it to find the field at the centre and on the axis of a circular coil
Apply Ampere’s circuital law to a long straight wire and a long solenoid, and use the formula for a finite straight wire

slides.heading: Moving Charges and Magnetic Field
slides.body_md: Part 1 — currents make magnetic fields: how to define B, and how to calculate it for wires, coils and solenoids.

visual.alt: Flow of this part: Oersted’s observation, the definition of B, the Biot–Savart law, the circular coil and Ampere’s circuital law

slides.narration: Every electric motor, loudspeaker and hospital scanner depends on one fact: an electric current produces a magnetic field. In this part we see the experiment that revealed it, define the magnetic field precisely from the force it exerts on a moving charge, and learn two tools for calculating it, the Biot Savart law and Ampere’s circuital law.

slides.heading: Oersted’s observation
slides.body_md: In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted noticed that a compass needle placed near a wire **deflected** whenever a current flowed, and **reversed** its deflection when the current was reversed.
bullets: A current (moving charge) produces a **magnetic field** around it.
The field lines of a straight wire are **circles** round the wire (right-hand grip rule: thumb along I, fingers curl along B).
Electricity and magnetism are linked: the start of electromagnetism.

slides.narration: Lay a wire north to south just above a compass. With no current the needle points north. Switch on a current flowing north and the north pole of the needle swings towards the west; reverse the current and it swings east. So the current creates a magnetic field, and the direction of that field depends on the direction of the current. Grip the wire with your right hand, thumb along the current: your fingers curl the way the field goes.

slides.heading: Defining the magnetic field B
slides.body_md:
A charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec v$ through a magnetic field feels a force
$$\vec F = q\left(\vec v \times \vec B\right),\qquad F = qvB\sin\theta$$
This defines $\vec B$: its size is $B = \dfrac{F}{qv\sin\theta}$, and $\vec F$ is perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\vec B$.
bullets: SI unit: **tesla** (T): 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹. The gauss, 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T, is also met.
No force if the charge is at rest or moves along $\vec B$; largest force, $qvB$, when $\vec v \perp \vec B$.

slides.narration: We define the magnetic field by what it does. A charge moving through the field feels a force q v cross B: its size is q v B sine theta, and it points at right angles to both the velocity and the field. So the field strength is the force per unit charge per unit speed, when the charge moves at right angles to the field. The unit is the tesla, a newton per ampere metre.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: measuring B from a force
slides.body_md: A dust grain carrying a charge of 5.0 nC moves at 400 m s$^{-1}$ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field and feels a force of $6.0 \times 10^{-8}$ N. Find B, and the force if the grain moved at $30^\circ$ to the field at the same speed.
bullets: Step 1 — $B = \dfrac{F}{qv} = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-8}}{5.0 \times 10^{-9} \times 400} = 0.030$ T.
Step 2 — $F = qvB\sin 30^\circ = 5.0 \times 10^{-9} \times 400 \times 0.030 \times 0.5 = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}$ N, half as much.

visual.alt: Worked table: the force on the grain is six times ten to the minus eight newton at ninety degrees, half that at thirty degrees and zero along the field

slides.narration: Divide the force by the charge times the speed: six times ten to the minus eight, over five nanocoulombs times four hundred, gives three hundredths of a tesla. If the grain crossed the field at thirty degrees instead, the sine of thirty is one half, so the force halves. Moving along the field lines, it would feel no magnetic force at all.

slides.heading: The Biot–Savart law
slides.body_md:
A current element $I\,d\vec l$ produces at a point with position vector $\vec r$ (from the element) the field
$$d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,d\vec l \times \vec r}{r^3},\qquad dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$$
bullets: $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A⁻¹ (permeability of free space); $\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7}$.
$d\vec B$ is perpendicular to both $d\vec l$ and $\vec r$; it is zero along the line of the element ($\theta = 0$).
Like Coulomb’s law it is an inverse-square law; unlike it, the source is a vector and the field depends on the angle.

slides.narration: The Biot Savart law gives the field of a tiny piece of current. Its size is mu nought over four pi, times the current, times the length of the piece, times the sine of the angle, over the distance squared. Its direction is that of d l cross r, at right angles to both. Points straight ahead of or behind the element get no field at all. To find the field of a whole circuit, add up the contributions of all its elements.

slides.heading: Field at the centre of a circular coil
slides.body_md:
For a circular loop of radius $R$, every element is at distance $R$ from the centre and at $90^\circ$ to the line joining it to the centre, so every $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2}$ points the same way, along the axis. Adding round the loop ($\sum dl = 2\pi R$) and over $N$ turns:
$$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$$
bullets: Direction from the right-hand grip rule: curl the fingers with the current; the thumb gives B at the centre.
Current anticlockwise as seen by you: B points towards you.

visual.caption: Directions computed from the Biot–Savart law: the parts across the axis cancel.

slides.narration: At the centre of a circular loop the geometry is as simple as it gets. Every element is the same distance R away and at right angles to the line to the centre, so every contribution has the same size and the same direction, along the axis. Adding them all, the lengths add up to the circumference, two pi R, which gives mu nought I over two R for one turn, and N times that for N turns.

slides.heading: Field on the axis of a circular coil
slides.body_md:
At a point on the axis, a distance $x$ from the centre, the components of $d\vec B$ across the axis cancel in pairs and the axial components add:
$$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2\left(R^2 + x^2\right)^{3/2}}$$
bullets: At $x = 0$ this gives the centre value $\mu_0NI/2R$.
Far away ($x \gg R$): $B \approx \mu_0NIR^2/2x^3$, falling as $1/x^3$.
B along the axis points the same way on both sides of the coil.

x.label: distance from the centre along the axis, x/R

y.label: B as a fraction of its centre value

visual.alt: Axial field of a flat circular coil as a fraction of its value at the centre: a single peak at the centre, about half at three quarters of a radius and falling towards zero far away on either side
visual.caption: At x = 0.75R the field is 0.8³ = 0.512 of the centre value (worked example 2).

slides.narration: Away from the centre, each element is a distance root R squared plus x squared from the point, and its field is tilted. Pair each element with the one opposite: their tilted components across the axis cancel, while the parts along the axis add. The result is mu nought N I R squared over two times R squared plus x squared to the power three halves. It peaks at the centre and falls off as the inverse cube far away.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a flat coil
slides.body_md: A flat coil of 40 turns and radius 8.0 cm carries 0.60 A. Find the field at its centre and at a point on its axis 6.0 cm from the centre.
bullets: Centre: $B_0 = \dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 40 \times 0.60}{2 \times 0.080} = 1.88 \times 10^{-4}$ T.
Ratio $B/B_0 = \left(\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}\right)^3 = 0.80^3 = 0.512$.

x.label: distance from the centre along the axis, x/R

y.label: B as a fraction of its centre value

visual.alt: Axial field of a flat circular coil as a fraction of its value at the centre: a single peak at the centre, about half at three quarters of a radius and falling towards zero far away on either side
visual.caption: At x = 0.75R the field is 0.8³ = 0.512 of the centre value (worked example 2).

slides.narration: At the centre, mu nought times forty turns times point six ampere, over sixteen centimetres, gives about one point nine times ten to the minus four tesla. Six centimetres along the axis, the distance to the windings is ten centimetres, a neat three four five triangle, and the field drops to about nine point six five times ten to the minus five tesla: just over half the centre value, as the graph shows.

slides.heading: Ampere’s circuital law
slides.body_md:
Round any closed loop, the line integral of $\vec B$ equals $\mu_0$ times the net current threading the loop:
$$\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}$$
**Long straight wire:** on a circle of radius $r$ about the wire, B is tangential and constant, so $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0I$ and
$$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$
bullets: Currents outside the loop add nothing; currents through it in opposite senses count with opposite signs.
The law is always true, but it gives B easily only when symmetry makes B constant along a well-chosen loop.

slides.narration: Ampere’s circuital law is a shortcut for symmetric currents. Go round any closed path, adding B along the path times each small step: the total is mu nought times the current passing through the path. Round a long straight wire, choose a circle centred on it. B is the same all the way round and along the path, so B times two pi r equals mu nought I, and B is mu nought I over two pi r.

slides.heading: Field of a long solenoid
slides.body_md:
A **solenoid** is a long coil of closely wound turns. Inside a long solenoid, away from its ends, the field is **uniform** and along the axis:
$$B = \mu_0 n I,\qquad n = \dfrac{N}{L}\ \text{(turns per metre)}$$
bullets: Outside, the field is very weak; the ends act like the N and S poles of a bar magnet.
B does not depend on the radius of the turns, only on the turns per metre and the current.
Applying Ampere’s law to a rectangular loop with one side inside gives $BL = \mu_0 NI$, the same result.

slides.narration: Wind wire closely round a long tube and pass a current: the fields of the turns add up inside to a strong, uniform field along the axis, while outside they nearly cancel. The field inside is mu nought n I, where n is the number of turns per metre. It does not depend on how fat the solenoid is. One end behaves as a north pole and the other as a south pole, just like a bar magnet.

slides.heading: A straight wire of finite length
slides.body_md:
For a straight wire carrying current $I$, and a point P at perpendicular distance $a$ from it, with the ends subtending angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ at P (measured from the perpendicular):
$$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}\left(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta\right)$$
bullets: Formula only (its derivation is not required in the ISC scope).
Very long wire: $\alpha, \beta \to 90^\circ$, so $B = \mu_0I/2\pi a$, as Ampere’s law gives.
Point opposite one end of a long wire: $\alpha = 0$, $\beta \to 90^\circ$, so $B = \mu_0I/4\pi a$.

The field is mu nought I over four pi a, times the sum of the sines of those two angles. Make the wire very long and both angles approach ninety degrees, so the bracket becomes two and we recover the long-wire result.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a cable and a solenoid
slides.body_md: (a) Find the field 3.0 cm from a long straight cable carrying 12 A. (b) A solenoid 40 cm long has 800 turns and carries 1.5 A. Find the field near its middle.
bullets: (a) $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 12}{0.030} = 8.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T (about twice the Earth’s field).

The solenoid has two thousand turns per metre, so its field is about three point seven seven millitesla, nearly fifty times stronger.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a short straight wire
slides.body_md: A straight wire 8.0 cm long carries 5.0 A. Find the field at a point 3.0 cm from its midpoint, on the perpendicular bisector, and compare it with the long-wire value.
bullets: Each end subtends $\sin\alpha = \sin\beta = \dfrac{4.0}{\sqrt{4.0^2 + 3.0^2}} = 0.80$.
$B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi a}(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta) = \dfrac{10^{-7} \times 5.0}{0.030} \times 1.6 = 2.67 \times 10^{-5}$ T.
A long wire would give $\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi a} = 3.33 \times 10^{-5}$ T, so the short wire gives 0.80 of it.

visual.caption: Once the wire is a few times longer than the distance a, the long-wire formula is a good approximation.

slides.narration: Half the wire is four centimetres and the point is three centimetres away, so each end sits on a three four five triangle and each sine is point eight. Ten to the minus seven times five amperes over three centimetres, times one point six, gives about two point six seven times ten to the minus five tesla: eight tenths of what an endless wire would give, as the graph shows.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: $\vec F = q(\vec v \times \vec B)$; $F = qvB\sin\theta$; tesla

visual.alt: Summary table of the definition of B, the Biot Savart law, the fields of a coil at its centre and on its axis, a long wire, a long solenoid and a finite wire

slides.narration: To sum up: a current makes a magnetic field, as Oersted found, and B is defined by the force q v cross B on a moving charge. The Biot Savart law gives the field of each current element; it leads to mu nought N I over two R at the centre of a coil. Ampere’s law gives mu nought I over two pi r for a long wire and mu nought n I inside a long solenoid.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Write the Biot–Savart law with the cross product and say what each symbol means.
Convert cm to m before substituting; remember $\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7}$ and $\mu_0/2\pi = 2 \times 10^{-7}$.
Coil questions: count the turns N; solenoid questions: use turns per metre n.
Give a direction with every field: right-hand grip rule.

rows: Distance from a long wire doubled?
Point along the line of an element?

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: State the Biot Savart law with its vector form and define every symbol. Always change centimetres to metres, and use the handy values ten to the minus seven for mu nought over four pi and two times ten to the minus seven for mu nought over two pi. For coils count the turns; for solenoids use turns per metre. And never give a field without its direction.

goals: Use the Lorentz force, explain why a magnetic force does no work, and describe circular and helical paths

slides.heading: Forces on moving charges and currents
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what a magnetic field does to moving charges and to the wires that carry them.

visual.alt: Flow of this part: the Lorentz force, circular and helical motion, crossed fields, the force on a wire, parallel currents and the definition of the ampere

slides.narration: In Part 1 currents made magnetic fields. Now we turn the question round: what does a magnetic field do to charges that move through it, and to wires that carry currents? The answers explain how the aurora forms, how beams are steered in particle accelerators, how motors turn, and how the ampere itself is defined.

slides.heading: The Lorentz force
slides.body_md:
In electric and magnetic fields together, a charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec v$ feels the **Lorentz force**
$$\vec F = q\left(\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B\right)$$
For a negative charge the magnetic force is opposite to the direction of $\vec v \times \vec B$.

visual.alt: Table of the magnetic force on a charge at rest, moving along the field, moving at right angles to it and moving at another angle, and the path that results in each case

slides.narration: The total force on a moving charge is the Lorentz force: q E, which acts whether or not the charge moves, plus q v cross B, which needs motion. The table shows the special cases. A charge at rest, or one moving along the field, feels no magnetic force. At right angles the force is largest and the path is a circle; at any other angle the path is a helix.

slides.heading: No work, so constant speed: circular motion
slides.body_md:
The magnetic force is always perpendicular to $\vec v$, so it does **no work**: $P = \vec F \cdot \vec v = 0$. The speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only the direction changes. If $\vec v \perp \vec B$, the force provides the centripetal force:
$$qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \;\Rightarrow\; r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{p}{qB},\qquad T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$$
bullets: T and the frequency $f = qB/2\pi m$ do not depend on the speed: faster particles move on bigger circles.

visual.alt: A positive charge moving in a circle in a field into the page, with the force towards the centre

slides.narration: Because the magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity, its power is zero: it can bend a path but never speed a particle up or slow it down. Moving at right angles to a uniform field, the particle feels a constant sideways force and goes round a circle. Equating q v B to m v squared over r gives the radius, m v over q B, and the time for one turn, two pi m over q B, which does not depend on the speed.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: an electron in a circle
slides.body_md: An electron moves at $4.0 \times 10^{6}$ m s$^{-1}$ at right angles to a uniform field of 2.0 mT. Find the radius of its path and its period. ($m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C)
bullets: $r = \dfrac{mv}{eB} = \dfrac{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 4.0 \times 10^{6}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.0114$ m (about 1.1 cm).
$T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}}{3.2 \times 10^{-22}} = 1.79 \times 10^{-8}$ s.

visual.alt: A positive charge moving in a circle in a field into the page, with the force towards the centre

slides.narration: The radius is the momentum over e B: about one point one four centimetres, small enough to fit inside a laboratory tube. The period is two pi m over e B, about one point eight times ten to the minus eight second, so the electron goes round more than fifty million times a second. Double its speed and the circle doubles in size, but the period stays exactly the same.

slides.narration: Compare the direction of the force with the direction of motion.

slides.heading: Helical motion
slides.body_md:
If $\vec v$ makes angle $\theta$ with $\vec B$, split it: $v_\perp = v\sin\theta$ gives circular motion, $v_\parallel = v\cos\theta$ is unaffected. The path is a **helix** about the field direction:
$$r = \dfrac{mv\sin\theta}{qB},\qquad \text{pitch } p = v\cos\theta \times T = \dfrac{2\pi m v\cos\theta}{qB}$$
bullets: Charged particles from the Sun spiral along the Earth’s field lines towards the poles, where they cause the aurora.

visual.alt: Side view of a helical path about the field direction, with its radius and pitch

slides.narration: At any other angle, split the velocity into two parts. The part across the field is bent into a circle, with radius m v sine theta over q B. The part along the field feels no force, so the particle drifts steadily along the field while it circles. The result is a helix, like a stretched spring. The pitch, the distance moved along the field in one turn, is the parallel speed times the period.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a proton on a helix
slides.body_md: A proton enters a uniform field of 0.10 T at $3.0 \times 10^{5}$ m s$^{-1}$, its velocity making $60^\circ$ with the field. Find the radius and pitch of its helix. ($m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg)
bullets: $v_\perp = 3.0 \times 10^{5}\sin 60^\circ = 2.60 \times 10^{5}$ m s$^{-1}$; $r = \dfrac{m v_\perp}{eB} = 0.0271$ m.
$T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB} = 6.56 \times 10^{-7}$ s; $v_\parallel = 3.0 \times 10^{5}\cos 60^\circ = 1.5 \times 10^{5}$ m s$^{-1}$.
Pitch $p = v_\parallel T = 1.5 \times 10^{5} \times 6.56 \times 10^{-7} = 0.0984$ m (about 9.8 cm).

visual.alt: Side view of a helical path about the field direction, with its radius and pitch

slides.narration: The speed across the field is three times ten to the five times the sine of sixty degrees, which gives a radius of about two point seven centimetres. One turn takes about six point six times ten to the minus seven second. Meanwhile the proton drifts along the field at half its speed, so each turn carries it about nine point eight centimetres further along the helix.

slides.heading: Crossed electric and magnetic fields
slides.body_md:
With $\vec E \perp \vec B$, both perpendicular to $\vec v$, the electric and magnetic forces can be opposite. The charge goes straight through when $qE = qvB$:
$$v = \dfrac{E}{B}$$
bullets: The result does not depend on q or m: the arrangement selects one speed (a **velocity selector**).
Faster charges are bent one way (magnetic force wins), slower ones the other.

slides.narration: Now put an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles. On a positive charge moving across both, the electric force pushes one way and the magnetic force the other. They balance when q E equals q v B, that is when the speed is E over B. Particles of exactly that speed fly straight through, whatever their charge or mass, while all others are bent aside.

slides.heading: Force on a current-carrying conductor
slides.body_md:
A wire of length $l$ and cross-section $A$ holds $nAl$ free electrons drifting at $v_d$. Each feels $e v_d B\sin\theta$, so the total is $(nAl)e v_d B\sin\theta$, and with $I = nAev_d$:
$$\vec F = I\left(\vec l \times \vec B\right),\qquad F = BIl\sin\theta$$
bullets: $\vec l$ points along the current. The force is largest when the wire is perpendicular to B and zero when it is parallel.
Direction: perpendicular to both the wire and B (the rule for $\vec l \times \vec B$).

slides.narration: A current is just charges on the move, so a wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels the sum of the forces on all its drifting electrons. Counting them, n A l electrons each with force e v d B sine theta, and using I equals n A e v d, the total becomes B I l sine theta. In vector form it is I l cross B, at right angles to both the wire and the field.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a wire in the Earth’s field
slides.body_md: A horizontal wire 60 cm long carries 5.0 A from west to east at a place where the Earth’s field is $4.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T, horizontal and pointing north. Find the size and direction of the force on the wire.
bullets: $F = BIl = 4.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 5.0 \times 0.60 = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}$ N.
Direction: $\vec l$ east, $\vec B$ north; with x east, y north, z up, $\hat x \times \hat y = \hat z$: the force is **vertically upwards**.

visual.alt: A straight conductor carrying current in a field into the page, with the force on it

slides.narration: The wire is at right angles to the field, so the force is simply B I l: four times ten to the minus five, times five amperes, times point six metre, about one point two times ten to the minus four newton. East crossed with north points straight up, so the Earth’s field pushes the wire gently upwards. Reverse the current and the push is downwards.

slides.heading: Force between parallel currents
slides.body_md:
Wire 1 makes a field $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1}{2\pi r}$ at wire 2, perpendicular to it. A length $l$ of wire 2 feels $F = B_1I_2l$, so the force per unit length is
$$f = \dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$$
bullets: **Like** (same direction) currents **attract**; **unlike** currents **repel**.
Wire 1 feels an equal and opposite force (Newton’s third law), even if $I_1 \ne I_2$.

The field of wire one at wire two is mu nought I one over two pi r, at right angles to wire two, so each metre of wire two feels mu nought I one I two over two pi r. Working out I l cross B shows that currents in the same direction pull the wires together, and opposite currents push them apart. The forces on the two wires are always equal and opposite.

bullets: Opposite currents: the leads **repel**; each metre of either lead feels the same $2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ N.

slides.heading: Defining the ampere and the coulomb
slides.body_md: For $I_1 = I_2 = 1$ A and $r = 1$ m in vacuum: $f = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1 \times 1}{2\pi \times 1} = 2 \times 10^{-7}$ N m$^{-1}$. This gives the definitions:
bullets: Since 2019 the SI fixes the value of the electron charge exactly; the parallel-wire result is still the standard definition asked for, and it gives $\mu_0 \approx 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A⁻¹.

rows: Steady current in each of two long, thin, parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum that makes each wire experience 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length
Charge carried past a cross-section in 1 s by a steady current of 1 A (1 C = 1 A s)

visual.alt: Table defining one ampere from the force between two parallel wires one metre apart, two times ten to the minus seven newton per metre, and one coulomb as one ampere second

slides.narration: Put one ampere in each of two long parallel wires one metre apart in vacuum, and each metre of wire feels two times ten to the minus seven newton. Turning this round gives the classic definition of the ampere. The coulomb then follows: it is the charge carried past any point in one second by a steady current of one ampere, so one coulomb is one ampere second.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: zero: speed and kinetic energy constant

visual.alt: Summary table of the Lorentz force, the work done by a magnetic force, circular and helical paths, crossed fields, the force on a conductor and between parallel wires

slides.narration: To sum up: the Lorentz force is q times E plus v cross B. The magnetic part does no work, so it bends paths into circles of radius m v over q B, with a period independent of speed, or into helices. Crossed fields pass only the speed E over B. A wire feels I l cross B, and parallel wires feel mu nought I one I two over two pi r per metre, which defines the ampere.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: For directions, write the vectors along x, y, z and use $\hat x \times \hat y = \hat z$; reverse the answer for an electron.
In circle problems quote $r = mv/qB$ and say why the speed is constant.
For a helix, use $v\sin\theta$ for the radius and $v\cos\theta$ for the pitch.
State the ampere with all its conditions: long, thin, parallel, 1 m apart, vacuum, $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre.

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: For any direction question, set up axes and use the cross product, and remember to reverse the answer for a negative charge. In circular-motion answers, say clearly why the speed does not change. For a helix, sine theta goes with the radius and cos theta with the pitch. And when defining the ampere, give every condition: long, thin, parallel wires, one metre apart, in vacuum.

notes.title: Moving Charges and Magnetic Field — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Oersted’s experiment and the definition of B
sections.body_md:
- **Oersted (1820):** a compass needle near a current-carrying wire deflects, and the deflection reverses with the current: a current produces a **magnetic field**. Field lines of a straight wire are circles round it (right-hand grip rule).
- A charge q moving with velocity **v** in a field **B** feels $\vec F = q(\vec v \times \vec B)$, of size $qvB\sin\theta$, perpendicular to both **v** and **B**. This defines B: $B = F/(qv\sin\theta)$.
- Unit: **tesla**, 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹; 1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ T. No force on a charge at rest or moving along B.

key_terms.definition_md: Vector field defined by the force F = q(v × B) on a moving charge; unit tesla.
Field in which a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to the field feels 1 N.

sections.heading: 2. The Biot–Savart law
sections.body_md:
$d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,d\vec l \times \vec r}{r^3}$, size $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$, with $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A⁻¹.
- $d\vec B$ is perpendicular to the plane of $d\vec l$ and $\vec r$; zero along the line of the element.
- Compared with Coulomb’s law: both inverse-square and both obey superposition; but the source $I\,d\vec l$ is a vector, the field depends on $\sin\theta$ and is perpendicular to $\vec r$ (the electric field is along $\vec r$).

sections.heading: 3. Circular coil: centre and axis
sections.body_md:
- **Centre** of a coil of N turns, radius R: every element is at 90° to the line to the centre and at distance R, so $B = \dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R}$ along the axis (right-hand grip rule).
- **Axis**, distance x from the centre: components across the axis cancel in pairs; $B = \dfrac{\mu_0NIR^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$. Far away, $B \approx \mu_0NIR^2/2x^3$.
- Example: 40 turns, R = 8.0 cm, 0.60 A gives 1.88 × 10⁻⁴ T at the centre and 0.512 of that at x = 6.0 cm.

key_terms.definition_md: Curl the fingers of the right hand along the current; the thumb gives the field at the centre.

sections.heading: 4. Ampere’s circuital law and its uses
sections.body_md:
- $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}$ round any closed loop; currents outside do not count, opposite currents count with opposite signs. Useful when symmetry makes B constant along the loop.
- **Long straight wire:** $B = \mu_0I/2\pi r$, circles round the wire.
- **Long solenoid:** $B = \mu_0nI$ inside (n = turns per metre), uniform and along the axis; weak outside; independent of the radius.
- **Finite straight wire** (formula only): $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi a}(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta)$, angles from the perpendicular; long wire $\alpha = \beta = 90^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: Closed path chosen so that B is constant in size and along (or across) the path, making the line integral easy.
Long, closely wound coil; field inside μ₀nI.

sections.heading: 5. Lorentz force and the motion of charges
sections.body_md:
- $\vec F = q(\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B)$. The magnetic part is perpendicular to **v**, so it does **no work**: speed and kinetic energy stay constant.
- $\vec v \perp \vec B$: circle, $r = mv/qB$, $T = 2\pi m/qB$ (independent of v), $f = qB/2\pi m$.
- At angle θ: helix, $r = mv\sin\theta/qB$, pitch $p = 2\pi mv\cos\theta/qB$. Along B: straight line.
- Crossed E and B: undeflected when $v = E/B$ (velocity selector).

key_terms.definition_md: Total force q(E + v × B) on a charge moving in electric and magnetic fields.
Distance a charge on a helix moves along the field in one revolution.

sections.heading: 6. Forces on currents; the ampere and the coulomb
sections.body_md:
- Conductor of length l: $\vec F = I(\vec l \times \vec B)$, $F = BIl\sin\theta$ (from $nAl$ electrons each feeling $ev_dB\sin\theta$, with $I = nAev_d$). Zero when the wire is along B.
- Parallel wires: $f = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}$ per unit length; like currents **attract**, unlike **repel**; equal and opposite forces.
- **Ampere:** the steady current in each of two long, thin, parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum that gives a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre. **Coulomb:** the charge carried in 1 s by 1 A (1 C = 1 A s).

key_terms.definition_md: Current in each of two long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum giving 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre between them.
Charge passing a point in 1 s when the current is 1 A.

questions.stem_md: A compass needle rests just below a horizontal wire. When a steady current is switched on in the wire the needle swings round, and when the current is reversed it swings the other way. This shows that

options.text_md: the wire has become a permanent magnet
the current exerts an electric force on the needle
the Earth’s magnetic field reverses near a current
a current in a wire sets up a magnetic field around it

questions.solution_md: The needle responds to a magnetic field produced by the moving charges in the wire (Oersted, 1820); reversing the current reverses that field — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A straight wire is stretched north–south a few centimetres above a horizontal compass needle. State, with a reason, which way the north pole of the needle swings when a current flows (a) northwards, (b) southwards in the wire.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) With x east, y north and z up, the needle is **below** the wire, so $\vec B \propto \hat y \times (-\hat z) = -\hat x$: the field at the needle points **west**, and the N pole swings **towards the west**. (b) Reversing the current reverses the field, so the N pole swings **towards the east**.

questions.solution_md: Right-hand grip rule below the wire.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Field below the wire points west: N pole swings west
(b) Current reversed: N pole swings east

questions.stem_md: A field in which a 1 C charge moving at 1 m s⁻¹ at right angles to the field lines feels a force of 1 N has a strength of one ___ (name the unit).
questions.solution_md: One **tesla** (T), since $B = F/qv$.

questions.stem_md: A charged pellet carrying 4.0 μC crosses a uniform magnetic field at right angles at 250 m s⁻¹ and experiences a sideways force of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ N. Find the magnetic field, in tesla.
A doubly charged ion (charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T. Find the magnetic force on it, in units of 10⁻¹⁵ N.
questions.solution_md: $F = qvB\sin\theta = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.0 \times 10^{5} \times 0.25 \times \sin 30^\circ = 8.0 \times 10^{-15}$ N, i.e. $\dfrac{8.0 \times 10^{-15}}{10^{-15}} = 8.0$.

questions.stem_md: A beam of protons passes through a region containing only a uniform magnetic field and emerges with its velocity completely unchanged. The protons must have been moving

options.text_md: at right angles to the field
at 45° to the field
parallel or antiparallel to the field
in any direction, since a magnetic field never acts on protons

questions.solution_md: F = qvB sin θ is zero only for θ = 0° or 180°; at any other angle the path bends — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A short current element at the origin carries current in the +x direction. By the Biot–Savart law, the field it produces at a point on the positive y-axis points in the

options.text_md: −z direction
+z direction
+y direction
−x direction

questions.solution_md: $d\vec B \propto d\vec l \times \vec r = \hat x \times \hat y = \hat z$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is equivalent to one tesla, the SI unit of magnetic field?

options.text_md: one newton per coulomb (N C⁻¹)
one newton per ampere per metre (N A⁻¹ m⁻¹)
one newton ampere per metre (N A m⁻¹)
one volt per metre (V m⁻¹)

questions.solution_md: From F = BIl, B = F/Il, so 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ (N C⁻¹ and V m⁻¹ are units of electric field) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Write the Biot–Savart law in vector form for the field produced by a current element, explain each symbol, and state the direction of the field.

answer.model_answer_md: $d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,d\vec l \times \vec r}{r^3}$, where $I\,d\vec l$ is the **current element** (along the current), $\vec r$ is the **position vector** of the field point from the element and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A⁻¹. $d\vec B$ is **perpendicular to both** $d\vec l$ and $\vec r$, as the cross product gives.

questions.solution_md: Vector form; symbols; direction.

marking_scheme.step: Vector form with μ₀/4π and r³
Symbols explained; dB ⊥ dl and r

questions.stem_md: Give two similarities and two differences between the Biot–Savart law for a current element and Coulomb’s law for the field of a point charge.

answer.model_answer_md: **Similarities:** both fields fall off as the **inverse square** of distance, and both are **linear in their source**, so fields of many sources add by superposition. **Differences:** the source of the electric field is a **scalar** charge q, but the magnetic source $I\,d\vec l$ is a **vector**, so dB depends on the **angle** θ ($\sin\theta$ factor); the electric field points **along** $\vec r$, while $d\vec B$ is **perpendicular** to $\vec r$.

questions.solution_md: Inverse-square and superposition; vector source and angle; direction relative to r.

marking_scheme.step: Difference: vector source, sin θ dependence
Difference: E along r, dB perpendicular to r

questions.stem_md: A straight wire carries 10 A. Find the size of the field produced by a 2.0 mm length of it at a point 20 cm away, on a line making 30° with the direction of the current. Give the answer in units of 10⁻⁸ T.

marking_scheme.step: Biot–Savart with sin 30° and r = 0.20 m

questions.stem_md: True or false? A short segment of a current-carrying wire produces no magnetic field at points lying on the straight line that extends the segment, in front of it or behind it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. On that line $d\vec l$ and $\vec r$ are parallel or antiparallel, so $\sin\theta = 0$ and $d\vec B = 0$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The magnetic force on a charged particle is always perpendicular to the magnetic field at its position.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic force on a moving charge is q(v × B), and a cross product is perpendicular to each of the two vectors in it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: q(v × B) is perpendicular to B (and to v) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A flat circular coil of 25 turns and radius 4.0 cm carries 0.80 A. Find the magnetic field at its centre, in units of 10⁻⁴ T (3 significant figures).
A coil of 10 turns and radius 3.0 cm carries 2.0 A. Find the magnetic field at a point on its axis 4.0 cm from its centre, in μT (3 significant figures).
Coil P has 1 turn of radius R and coil Q has 3 turns of radius 3R; both carry the same current. The ratio of the field at the centre of P to that at the centre of Q is
questions.solution_md: B = μ₀NI/2R ∝ N/R: for P, 1/R; for Q, 3/3R = 1/R. The fields are equal — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A fixed length of wire carrying a steady current is first bent into a single circular turn and then rewound into a flat coil of 2 turns. The field at the centre becomes

options.text_md: 2 times as large
4 times as large
the same
8 times as large

questions.solution_md: The length is fixed, so with 2 turns the radius halves. B ∝ N/R gives 2 ÷ ½ = 4 times — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A circular loop lies in the plane of this page and carries a current that flows clockwise as you look at it. At the centre of the loop the magnetic field is

options.text_md: perpendicular to the page, pointing into it (away from you)
perpendicular to the page, pointing out of it (towards you)
in the plane of the page, along a diameter
zero, because opposite sides of the loop cancel

questions.solution_md: Curl the right-hand fingers clockwise: the thumb points into the page. Every element contributes in the same direction, so nothing cancels — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Using the Biot–Savart law, obtain the magnetic field at the centre of a flat circular coil of N turns and radius R carrying a current I, and state its direction.

answer.model_answer_md: Every element $d\vec l$ of a turn is at distance $R$ from the centre and **perpendicular** to the line joining it to the centre ($\theta = 90^\circ$), so $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2}$, and all the $d\vec B$ point the **same way, along the axis**. Adding round one turn, $\sum dl = 2\pi R$: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I (2\pi R)}{4\pi R^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}$. For N turns $B = \dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R}$, along the axis as given by the **right-hand grip rule**.

questions.solution_md: θ = 90° for every element; all dB parallel; sum of dl = 2πR.

marking_scheme.step: dB = μ₀I dl/4πR², all along the axis
N turns: μ₀NI/2R; direction by right-hand rule

questions.stem_md: A flat circular coil of 50 turns and radius 10 cm stands vertically with its plane at right angles to the magnetic meridian. What current through it would make the field at its centre exactly cancel the horizontal component of the Earth’s field, 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ T? Give the answer in amperes (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: The coil’s axis lies along the meridian, so its central field can oppose the Earth’s horizontal field: $\dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R} = B_H$ gives $I = \dfrac{2RB_H}{\mu_0N} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.10 \times 3.6 \times 10^{-5}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 50} = 0.115$ A (in the sense that makes the central field point south).

questions.stem_md: On the axis of a flat circular coil, at a distance from the centre equal to twice the coil’s radius, the field is what fraction of the field at the centre? Give the answer to 2 significant figures.

**Assertion (A):** Doubling the current in a flat circular coil doubles the magnetic field at its centre.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic field at the centre of a flat circular coil is inversely proportional to its radius.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true (B = μ₀NI/2R), but R, about the dependence on radius, does not explain why B doubles with the current — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Starting from the field on the axis of a flat circular coil, show that at distances x much greater than its radius R the field varies as 1/x³. What does the same expression give at x = 0?

answer.model_answer_md: On the axis $B = \dfrac{\mu_0NIR^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$. For $x \gg R$, $R^2 + x^2 \approx x^2$, so $B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0NIR^2}{2x^3}$: **B falls as 1/x³**. At $x = 0$ it gives $\dfrac{\mu_0NIR^2}{2R^3} = \dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R}$, the **centre value**.

questions.solution_md: Neglect R² against x²; set x = 0.

questions.stem_md: Find the magnetic field 8.0 cm from a long straight conductor carrying 20 A, in μT.
At what distance from a long straight wire carrying 3.0 A is the magnetic field 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ T? Give the answer in cm.

Four long straight wires run perpendicular to the page. Three of them pass through a closed loop drawn on the page, carrying 4 A out of the page, 6 A out of the page and 3 A into the page; the fourth, carrying 5 A out of the page, lies outside the loop. The value of $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l$ round the loop, in T m, is
questions.solution_md: Only currents threading the loop count, with signs: $I_{\text{enc}} = 4 + 6 - 3 = 7$ A, so $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = 7\mu_0$. The outside 5 A wire contributes nothing to the integral — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Point P is 2.0 cm from a long straight wire carrying current I, and point Q is 4.0 cm from another long straight wire carrying current 3I. The ratio of the field at P to the field at Q is
questions.solution_md: B ∝ I/r: at P, I/2; at Q, 3I/4. Ratio (1/2) : (3/4) = 2 : 3 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A long solenoid 30 cm long has 600 turns and carries 0.50 A. Find the magnetic field near its middle, in mT (3 significant figures).
A long solenoid is wound with 15 turns per centimetre. What current must it carry to produce a field of 6.0 mT inside it? Give the answer in amperes (3 significant figures).
A long solenoid is gently stretched until its length doubles, keeping the same number of turns and the same current. The field near its middle

options.text_md: doubles
stays the same, since N and I are unchanged
falls to half its original value
falls to a quarter of its original value

questions.solution_md: B = μ₀nI with n = N/L: doubling L halves n, so B halves — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A straight wire 6.0 cm long carries 4.0 A. Find the magnetic field at a point 4.0 cm from the midpoint of the wire, on its perpendicular bisector, in μT.
questions.solution_md: Each half is 3.0 cm, so $\sin\alpha = \sin\beta = \dfrac{3.0}{\sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.0^2}} = 0.60$. $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi a}(\sin\alpha + \sin\beta) = \dfrac{10^{-7} \times 4.0}{0.040} \times 1.2 = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ T, i.e. $1.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{6} = 12\ \mu$T.

questions.stem_md: The field of a straight wire of finite length at perpendicular distance a is B = (μ₀I/4πa)(sin α + sin β). Show that it reduces to μ₀I/2πa for a very long wire, and find B at perpendicular distance a from the end of a very long wire that extends in one direction only.

answer.model_answer_md: Very long wire: both ends are far away, so $\alpha, \beta \to 90^\circ$ and $\sin\alpha + \sin\beta \to 2$: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi a} \times 2 = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi a}$. Opposite the end of a semi-infinite wire, $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta \to 90^\circ$: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi a}$, **half** the long-wire value.

questions.solution_md: Angles 90° and 90°; then 0° and 90°.

questions.stem_md: A square loop of wire of side 10 cm carries a current of 5.0 A. Using the formula for the field of a finite straight wire, find the magnetic field at the centre of the square.

answer.model_answer_md: Each side is at perpendicular distance $a = 5.0$ cm from the centre, and its ends subtend $\alpha = \beta = 45^\circ$. One side gives $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{4\pi a}(\sin 45^\circ + \sin 45^\circ) = \dfrac{10^{-7} \times 5.0}{0.050} \times \sqrt2 = 1.41 \times 10^{-5}$ T. All four sides give fields in the **same direction** (perpendicular to the loop), so $B = 4B_1 = 5.66 \times 10^{-5}$ T.

questions.solution_md: a = side/2; α = β = 45°; four equal contributions add.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Moving from 2 cm to 4 cm away from a long straight current-carrying wire halves the magnetic field.

**Reason (R):** On a circle centred on the wire, B is tangential and constant in size, so Ampere’s law gives B(2πr) = μ₀I.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: B = μ₀I/2πr ∝ 1/r, so doubling r halves B — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State Ampere’s circuital law. In applying it, how are currents that thread the loop in opposite directions, and currents that do not pass through the loop, treated?

answer.model_answer_md: $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}$: the line integral of B round **any closed loop** equals $\mu_0$ times the **net current threading** the loop. Currents through the loop in opposite senses take **opposite signs** (the right-hand rule fixes the positive sense); currents **outside** the loop add **nothing** to the integral, though they do affect B on the loop.

questions.solution_md: Statement; signs; outside currents.

marking_scheme.step: Statement with μ₀ × net enclosed current
Opposite currents: opposite signs; outside currents: no contribution

questions.stem_md: Use Ampere’s circuital law to find the magnetic field at a distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I, explaining why you choose the closed path you do.

answer.model_answer_md: By symmetry the field lines are **circles centred on the wire**, and B has the same size at every point a distance r away. So choose as the Amperian loop a **circle of radius r** centred on the wire: at every point B is **along** $d\vec l$ and **constant**, so $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = B(2\pi r)$. The current threading the loop is I, so $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0I$ and $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}$, tangential to the circle.

questions.solution_md: Symmetry; circular loop; B(2πr) = μ₀I.

marking_scheme.step: Symmetry: circular field lines, constant B at fixed r

questions.stem_md: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 6.0 A and 4.0 A in the same direction. How far from the 6.0 A wire, on the line between the wires, is the magnetic field zero? Give the answer in cm.
questions.solution_md: Between like currents the two fields are opposite, so they cancel where $\dfrac{\mu_0 \times 6.0}{2\pi x} = \dfrac{\mu_0 \times 4.0}{2\pi(0.10 - x)}$: $6.0(0.10 - x) = 4.0x$, so $x = 0.060$ m $= 6.0$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: Fields opposite between like currents: 6/x = 4/(0.10 − x)
x = 6.0 cm from the 6.0 A wire

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Near the middle of a long, closely wound solenoid the magnetic field is μ₀nI, directed along the axis.

**Reason (R):** The field of a long solenoid is strongest just outside its windings.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: outside a long solenoid the field is very weak; it is strong and uniform inside — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A uniform magnetic field can change the direction in which a proton moves but cannot change its kinetic energy.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic force on a moving charge is always perpendicular to its velocity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: a force perpendicular to v does no work (F·v = 0), so the speed and kinetic energy stay constant — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An alpha particle (charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 1.6 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.75 T. Find the radius of its path, in cm.
Find the frequency with which an electron circles in a uniform magnetic field of 5.0 mT, in MHz (3 significant figures). (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{eB}{2\pi m_e} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2\pi \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = 1.40 \times 10^{8}$ Hz, i.e. $\dfrac{1.40 \times 10^{8}}{10^{6}} = 140$ MHz (whatever the electron’s speed).

questions.stem_md: A proton and an alpha particle (charge 2e, mass 4mₚ) are each accelerated from rest through the same potential difference and then move at right angles to the same uniform magnetic field. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle’s path to that of the proton’s is
questions.solution_md: $qV = \tfrac12mv^2$ gives $mv = \sqrt{2mqV}$, so $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{1}{B}\sqrt{\dfrac{2mV}{q}} \propto \sqrt{m/q}$. For the alpha particle $m/q$ is $4/2 = 2$ times the proton’s, so the ratio is $\sqrt2 : 1$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An ion moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The field is then doubled while the ion’s speed stays the same. Its new circular path has

options.text_md: half the radius and the same period
twice the radius and twice the period
the same radius and half the period
half the radius and half the period

questions.solution_md: r = mv/qB and T = 2πm/qB both vary as 1/B — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A proton moves vertically upwards through a horizontal magnetic field that points due north. The magnetic force on it is directed towards the

options.text_md: west
east
north
south

questions.solution_md: With x east, y north and z up: $\vec v \times \vec B \propto \hat z \times \hat y = -\hat x$, which is west; the proton is positive — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An electron travels due east through a magnetic field that points vertically upwards. The magnetic force on the electron points

options.text_md: due south
vertically downwards
due north
due west

questions.solution_md: With x east, y north and z up: $\vec v \times \vec B \propto \hat x \times \hat z = -\hat y$ (south). The electron’s charge is negative, so the force is reversed: due north — option (c).

questions.stem_md: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field of 2.0 mT with a speed of 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, its velocity making 30° with the field. Find the pitch of its helical path, in cm (3 significant figures). (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.solution_md: $T = \dfrac{2\pi m_e}{eB} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.79 \times 10^{-8}$ s. Pitch $p = v\cos 30^\circ \times T = 3.0 \times 10^{6} \times 0.866 \times 1.79 \times 10^{-8} = 0.0464$ m $= 4.64$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: p = v cos θ × T ≈ 4.64 cm

questions.stem_md: Describe, with a reason in each case, the path of a charged particle that enters a uniform magnetic field (a) moving along the field lines, (b) at right angles to them, (c) at 45° to them.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **Straight line** at constant speed: $\theta = 0$, so $qvB\sin\theta = 0$ and there is no force. (b) **Circle** in a plane perpendicular to B: the force $qvB$ has constant size and is always perpendicular to v, so it acts as a centripetal force ($r = mv/qB$). (c) **Helix** about the field direction: $v\sin 45^\circ$ is bent into a circle while $v\cos 45^\circ$, along B, is unaffected.

questions.solution_md: sin θ = 0; constant perpendicular force; split the velocity.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Straight line: no force along B
(b) Circle: constant force perpendicular to v
(c) Helix: perpendicular part circles, parallel part unchanged

questions.stem_md: In a region of crossed fields, E = 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.060 T, arranged so that the electric and magnetic forces on a charge moving at right angles to both are opposite. At what speed does a charged particle pass through undeflected? Give the answer in units of 10⁵ m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $qE = qvB \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{E}{B} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{4}}{0.060} = 5.0 \times 10^{5}$ m s$^{-1}$, i.e. $\dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{5}}{10^{5}} = 5.0$, for any charge or mass.

questions.stem_md: A proton moves along +x at 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ through a region where an electric field of 1.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ points along +y and a magnetic field of 0.020 T points along +z. Find the size of the net force on the proton, in units of 10⁻¹⁶ N.
questions.solution_md: $\vec v \times \vec B = vB(\hat x \times \hat z) = -vB\,\hat y$, with $vB = 2.0 \times 10^{5} \times 0.020 = 4.0 \times 10^{3}$ V m$^{-1}$. So $\vec F = e(E - vB)\hat y = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times (1.0 \times 10^{4} - 4.0 \times 10^{3})\,\hat y = 9.6 \times 10^{-16}$ N along +y, i.e. $\dfrac{9.6 \times 10^{-16}}{10^{-16}} = 9.6$.

questions.stem_md: A particle of charge q and mass m is projected with speed v at right angles to a uniform magnetic field B. Obtain the radius of its orbit and the time for one revolution, and hence explain why all such particles with the same q/m take the same time to go round, whatever their speed.

answer.model_answer_md: The force $qvB$ is always perpendicular to v, so the speed is constant and the force supplies the **centripetal force**: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, giving $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$. The time for one revolution is $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$. T contains **no v**: a faster particle moves on a **proportionally larger** circle, so the time per turn depends only on $q/m$ and B.

questions.solution_md: Centripetal force; T = 2πr/v.

marking_scheme.step: T = 2πm/qB, independent of v (larger r for larger v)

questions.stem_md: A student proposes to speed up a beam of protons by passing it through a very strong steady magnetic field. Evaluate the proposal.

answer.model_answer_md: It **will not work**. The magnetic force $q\vec v \times \vec B$ is always **perpendicular to the velocity**, so it does **no work** ($\vec F \cdot \vec v = 0$): the protons’ **speed and kinetic energy stay the same**, and the field only **bends** the beam. To speed them up an **electric field** (a potential difference) is needed.

questions.solution_md: Magnetic force does no work.

marking_scheme.step: Force perpendicular to v: no work, speed unchanged
Only deflects; an electric field is needed to accelerate

questions.stem_md: A straight wire 40 cm long carries 2.5 A and lies at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Find the force on the wire, in newtons.
questions.solution_md: $F = BIl\sin\theta = 0.20 \times 2.5 \times 0.40 \times \sin 30^\circ = 0.10$ N.

questions.stem_md: A horizontal straight rod 0.50 m long, of mass 40 g, lies at right angles to a horizontal magnetic field of 0.25 T. What current in the rod would make the magnetic force on it just balance its weight? Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Give the answer in amperes (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: For balance $BIl = mg$, so $I = \dfrac{mg}{Bl} = \dfrac{0.040 \times 9.8}{0.25 \times 0.50} = \dfrac{0.392}{0.125} = 3.14$ A (in the direction that makes $I\vec l \times \vec B$ point upwards).

questions.stem_md: A straight wire carries a current due north through a magnetic field that points vertically downwards. The force on the wire points

options.text_md: due east
due west
due north
vertically upwards

questions.solution_md: With x east, y north and z up: $\vec F = I\vec l \times \vec B \propto \hat y \times (-\hat z) = -\hat x$, due west — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two long straight parallel wires 5.0 cm apart carry 12 A and 9.0 A in the same direction. Find the force on a 2.0 m length of either wire, in mN (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 12 \times 9.0}{0.050} = 4.32 \times 10^{-4}$ N m$^{-1}$; on 2.0 m, $F = 8.64 \times 10^{-4}$ N $= 0.864$ mN, attractive.

questions.stem_md: Two long straight wires lie side by side, one carrying 3.0 A and the other 6.0 A in the opposite direction. Compared with the force on the 6.0 A wire, the force on the 3.0 A wire is

options.text_md: equal in size, with the wires pushing apart
half as large, with the wires pulling together
twice as large, with the wires pushing apart
equal in size, with the wires pulling together

questions.solution_md: Each wire feels μ₀I₁I₂/2πr per metre, which contains both currents (Newton’s third law); unlike currents repel — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State the definition of one ampere based on the magnetic force between two long parallel wires in vacuum, and use it to define one coulomb.

answer.model_answer_md: One **ampere** is the steady current in each of two **long, thin, parallel** wires **1 m apart in vacuum** that makes each wire feel **2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre**. One **coulomb** is the charge carried past a point in **1 s** by a steady current of **1 A** (1 C = 1 A s).

questions.solution_md: Parallel-wire force; Q = It.

marking_scheme.step: Ampere: 1 m apart, vacuum, 2 × 10⁻⁷ N m⁻¹

questions.stem_md: Two long, thin, parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum carry equal steady currents, and each metre of either wire is pushed with a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N. Each current is then one ___.
questions.solution_md: One **ampere**: $\dfrac{\mu_0I^2}{2\pi \times 1} = 2 \times 10^{-7}$ N m$^{-1}$ gives $I = 1$ A.

questions.stem_md: True or false? One coulomb is the charge that a steady current of one ampere carries past a point in the circuit in one second.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Q = It, so 1 C = 1 A × 1 s.

questions.stem_md: Two long straight conductors in vacuum, a distance r apart, carry steady currents I₁ and I₂ in the same sense. Obtain the magnetic force on each metre of either conductor and show that the conductors attract.

answer.model_answer_md: Conductor 1 sets up a field $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1}{2\pi r}$ at conductor 2, **perpendicular** to it (circles round conductor 1). A length l of conductor 2 feels $F = B_1I_2l$, so $\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}$. By $I_2\vec l \times \vec B_1$ this force points **towards conductor 1**; by symmetry conductor 1 feels an equal force towards conductor 2: like currents **attract**.

questions.solution_md: B₁ at the second wire; F = B₁I₂l; direction by I l × B.

marking_scheme.step: Direction towards the other wire: attraction

questions.stem_md: Starting from the force on a single moving charge, show that a straight conductor of length l carrying current I in a uniform field B experiences a force F = I(l × B).

answer.model_answer_md: Let the conductor have cross-section A and n free electrons per unit volume drifting with velocity $\vec v_d$. Each feels $-e(\vec v_d \times \vec B)$; there are $nAl$ of them, so $\vec F = -nAle(\vec v_d \times \vec B)$. The current is $I = nAe v_d$, and $\vec l$ (in the direction of the current) is opposite to $\vec v_d$, so $-nAle\,\vec v_d = I\vec l$. Hence $\vec F = I(\vec l \times \vec B)$, of size $BIl\sin\theta$.

questions.solution_md: Sum over nAl drifting electrons; I = nAev_d.

marking_scheme.step: Force on one electron and number nAl
I = nAev_d; l along the current
F = I(l × B), size BIl sin θ

questions.stem_md: Parallel wires A and B are 8.0 cm apart and carry 10 A and 6.0 A in the same direction. A third parallel wire C, midway between them, carries 2.0 A in the same direction. Find the net force on each metre of C, in units of 10⁻⁵ N m⁻¹, and state which way it acts.
questions.solution_md: Each wire is 4.0 cm from C and all currents are alike, so C is pulled towards both. From A: $\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 10 \times 2.0}{0.040} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ N m$^{-1}$; from B: $\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 6.0 \times 2.0}{0.040} = 6.0 \times 10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$. Net $= 4.0 \times 10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$, i.e. $\dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-5}}{10^{-5}} = 4.0$, **towards A**.

marking_scheme.step: Forces from A and B opposite: 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ and 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ N m⁻¹

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A straight current-carrying wire experiences the largest magnetic force when it lies along the direction of a uniform magnetic field.

**Reason (R):** The force on a straight conductor of length l is BIl sin θ, where θ is the angle between the wire and the field.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: along the field θ = 0, so the force is zero; it is largest at θ = 90° — option (d).

questions.stem_md: (a) A flat circular coil of N turns and radius R carries a current I. Using the Biot–Savart law, obtain the magnetic field at a point on its axis a distance x from its centre. [3] (b) A coil of 200 turns and radius 10 cm carries 0.50 A. Find the field at its centre and at a point on its axis 24 cm from the centre. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An element $d\vec l$ is at distance $r = \sqrt{R^2 + x^2}$ from P and perpendicular to $\vec r$, so $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2 + x^2}$, perpendicular to $\vec r$. Pairing elements at opposite ends of a diameter, the components **across the axis cancel**; the **axial** components $dB\sin\phi$ with $\sin\phi = R/r$ add. So $B = \dfrac{\mu_0IR}{4\pi r^3}\sum dl = \dfrac{\mu_0IR(2\pi R)}{4\pi r^3} = \dfrac{\mu_0IR^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$, and for N turns $B = \dfrac{\mu_0NIR^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$, along the axis.

(b) Centre: $B_0 = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 200 \times 0.50}{2 \times 0.10} = 6.28 \times 10^{-4}$ T. At 24 cm: $\sqrt{R^2 + x^2} = \sqrt{0.010 + 0.0576} = 0.26$ m, so $B = B_0\left(\dfrac{0.10}{0.26}\right)^3 = 3.57 \times 10^{-5}$ T.

questions.solution_md: Biot–Savart; cancel across the axis; numbers.

marking_scheme.step: dB = μ₀I dl/4π(R² + x²), each element ⊥ r
Cross-axis parts cancel; axial parts dB·R/r add

questions.stem_md: (a) State Ampere’s circuital law and use it to obtain the magnetic field at a distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I. [2] (b) A straight wire 12 cm long carries 6.0 A. Find the field at a point 8.0 cm from its midpoint, on its perpendicular bisector. [1] (c) A solenoid 25 cm long with 500 turns carries 2.0 A. Find the field near its middle, and the current a single long straight wire would need to produce a field of the same size 1.0 cm from it. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0I_{\text{enc}}$. On a circle of radius r centred on the wire, B is tangential and constant, so $B(2\pi r) = \mu_0I$ and $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}$.

(b) $\sin\alpha = \sin\beta = \dfrac{6.0}{10} = 0.60$; $B = \dfrac{10^{-7} \times 6.0}{0.080} \times 1.2 = 9.0 \times 10^{-6}$ T.

(c) $n = \dfrac{500}{0.25} = 2000$ m$^{-1}$; $B = \mu_0nI = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2000 \times 2.0 = 5.03 \times 10^{-3}$ T. For the wire, $I = \dfrac{2\pi rB}{\mu_0} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 0.010 \times 5.03 \times 10^{-3}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}} \approx 251$ A: a solenoid gives a strong field from a small current.

questions.solution_md: Ampere’s law; finite-wire formula; solenoid.

questions.stem_md: (a) A charge q moves with velocity v through a region containing both an electric field E and a magnetic field B. Write the total force on it in vector form and show that the magnetic part cannot alter its speed. [2] (b) Electrons travelling at 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ are bent by a uniform magnetic field of 1.5 mT acting at right angles to the beam. Find the radius of their path and the time for one revolution. [2] (c) An electric field is now added so that the beam goes straight on. Find its size and say how it must be directed. [1] (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Lorentz force $\vec F = q(\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B)$. The magnetic part $q\vec v \times \vec B$ is perpendicular to $\vec v$, so its power $\vec F \cdot \vec v = 0$: it does no work, and the speed (kinetic energy) cannot change; only the direction does.

(b) $r = \dfrac{mv}{eB} = \dfrac{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.0 \times 10^{7}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.0758$ m (about 7.6 cm); $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{eB} = 2.38 \times 10^{-8}$ s.

(c) The net force must vanish: $\vec E = -\vec v \times \vec B$, of size $E = vB = 2.0 \times 10^{7} \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} = 3.0 \times 10^{4}$ V m$^{-1}$, perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\vec B$ (along $\vec B \times \vec v$), so that the electric force cancels the magnetic force.

questions.solution_md: Lorentz force; r and T; E = vB.

marking_scheme.step: Magnetic part ⊥ v: no work, speed constant
E = vB = 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹, along B × v

questions.stem_md: (a) Two long straight parallel conductors in vacuum, a distance r apart, carry currents I₁ and I₂. Find the force on a length l of one of them due to the other, and state when this force is attractive. [2] (b) Use your result to define the ampere. [1] (c) A long horizontal wire P carries 50 A. A second long wire Q, parallel to P and 2.0 cm directly below it, has a mass of 2.0 g per metre. What current in Q, and in which direction, would let the magnetic force support Q’s weight? Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) P’s field at Q is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1}{2\pi r}$, perpendicular to Q, so $F = BI_2l = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2l}{2\pi r}$. The force is **attractive** when the currents are in the **same** direction (repulsive when opposite).

(b) One ampere is the steady current in each of two long, thin, parallel conductors 1 m apart in vacuum that produces a force of $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre on each.

(c) Q must be pulled **up**, towards P, so its current is in the **same direction** as P’s. Per metre: $\dfrac{\mu_0I_PI_Q}{2\pi r} = (m/l)g$, so $I_Q = \dfrac{(m/l)g \times 2\pi r}{\mu_0I_P} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.8 \times 0.020}{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 50} = 39.2$ A.

questions.solution_md: Force between currents; ampere; balance with the weight.

marking_scheme.step: F = μ₀I₁I₂l/2πr; attractive for like currents
I_Q ≈ 39.2 A, same direction as P

questions.stem_md: (a) Show that a straight conductor of length l carrying a current I at an angle θ to a uniform magnetic field B experiences a force of size BIl sin θ, and state its direction. [2] (b) A metal rod of mass 15 g rests across two smooth horizontal rails 25 cm apart, in a vertical magnetic field of 0.30 T. A current of 4.0 A flows through the rod from one rail to the other. Find the force on the rod and its initial acceleration. [2] (c) State what happens if the current is reversed. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The conductor holds $nAl$ free electrons drifting at $v_d$, each feeling $ev_dB\sin\theta$; the total is $nAle\,v_dB\sin\theta = BIl\sin\theta$ since $I = nAe v_d$. In vector form $\vec F = I\vec l \times \vec B$: perpendicular to both the conductor and the field.

(b) The rod is perpendicular to B: $F = BIl = 0.30 \times 4.0 \times 0.25 = 0.30$ N, horizontal and along the rails. $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{0.30}{0.015} = 20$ m s$^{-2}$.

(c) The force reverses ($\vec l$ reverses in $I\vec l \times \vec B$), so the rod is pushed the other way along the rails with the same size of force.

questions.solution_md: Sum over electrons; F = BIl; a = F/m; reversal.

marking_scheme.step: Sum of forces on drifting electrons
